basics.title: What Is Leverage [Really?]
basics.description: Three short concepts. No jargon. Once you grasp these, you understand the foundation of every leveraged trade you'll ever place.

items.title: Leverage, defined
items.text: A multiplier that lets you control a position larger than the cash in your account, using your broker's borrowed capital as the rest.
items.example: With $1,000 at 1:100 leverage, you control a $100,000 position.

items.title: Margin, explained
items.text: The portion of your own funds locked as collateral to open and maintain a position. Higher leverage means a smaller margin requirement.
items.example: At 1 : 100, a $100,000 trade requires only 1% margin — just $1,000.

items.title: The double-edged sword
items.text: Leverage scales gains and losses equally. A 1% adverse move on a 1:100 position can erase your entire margin. Trade with care.
items.example: Risk warning: leveraged trading may result in losses. Use stop-loss orders.

items.a: Tiered leverage adjusts the CFD leverage ratio based on position size. For example, smaller positions may qualify for leverage up to 1:2000, while larger positions may move to lower leverage tiers and require additional margin.

items.q: Can tiered leverage affect my trading strategy?
items.a: Leverage in CFD trading can affect your strategy when trading larger positions. Higher margin requirements from tiered leverage may limit your ability to open additional positions or require you to adjust existing ones.

items.q: Is tiered leverage the same for all assets?
items.a: No. The CFD leverage ratio may vary across different asset classes. For example, forex pairs may have higher leverage ratios than commodities or indices, resulting in different margin requirements.

items.q: What happens if I can't meet the margin requirements due to tiered leverage?
items.a: If you cannot meet the margin requirements due to tiered leverage, you may need to add funds or adjust your position size to maintain sufficient margin for your CFD trades.
Yes, tiered leverage is typically applied automatically by the trading platform based on the size of your position.

items.q: How can I calculate the margin required with tiered leverage?
items.a: You can calculate forex margin using the margin calculator, which considers your position size, leverage tier, and applicable margin requirements.

a: HMR is a temporary increase in the margin required to open new trades during periods of elevated market risk such as daily rollover and major economic announcements.
It is a protective risk-management mechanism.

items.q: Why does my margin level drop even if price did not move?
a: During HMR, the required margin per position increases.
Because margin increases while equity remains the same, your margin level (%) decreases even if the market price has not changed.

items.q: Will my trade be closed because of HMR?
a: HMR itself does not close trades.
However, if the margin level falls to the platform stop-out level due to the temporary margin increase, the trading platform will automatically close positions according to normal trading rules.
Your trade price, stop loss, and take profit remain unchanged.
However, the margin required to maintain the position may temporarily increase, which can reduce free margin.
Spread changes are caused by market liquidity and pricing from liquidity providers, not by HMR.
HMR only changes the margin requirement.
